An activation normalization layer transforms intermediate numerical representations inside a network.
The key questions are **which coordinates share statistics**, **whether the mean is subtracted**, and **whether training and inference use the same statistics**.
This differs from [quantile scaling](quantile-normalization.qmd#quantile-scaling), which expresses physical input or output coordinates using fixed training-data reference values.

## Comparing normalization methods {#what-to-check-when-reading-a-model}

| Method | Training statistics | Inference statistics |
|---|---|---|
| [BatchNorm](#batchnorm) | Batch; also space for CNNs | Estimated population |
| [Token LayerNorm](#layernorm) | One token's hidden coordinates | Current token |
| [Token RMSNorm](#rmsnorm) | One token's hidden coordinates | Current token |

BatchNorm and LayerNorm subtract the mean; RMSNorm only rescales.
These rows describe common settings; the normalized axes remain part of the model specification.
The sections below give the equations for each method.

The learned affine transformation means that normalized layer outputs need not retain zero mean or unit variance.
Normalization also does not generally decorrelate features, make them Gaussian, or preserve information needed to invert the input from the output alone.
Placement matters: [ViT](../../literature-review/vision/vit.qmd) normalizes before attention and its MLP, while [LLaMA](../../literature-review/language/llama.qmd) uses RMSNorm before its transformer sublayers.
[PaliGemma](../../literature-review/language/paligemma.qmd) motivates keeping these activation operations distinct from image encoding, text tokenization, and physical-coordinate scaling.

## BatchNorm Uses Other Examples {#batchnorm}

For one feature, collect its values $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ across a training minibatch.
BatchNorm computes a mean and variance for that feature, normalizes it, and applies a learned scale $\gamma$ and offset $\beta$:

$$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mu_B&=\frac1m\sum_i x_i,\\
        v_B&=\frac1m\sum_i(x_i-\mu_B)^2,\\
        y_i&=\gamma\frac{x_i-\mu_B}{\sqrt{v_B+\epsilon}}+\beta.
    \end{aligned}
$$

In a convolutional layer, the original method pools over batch and spatial positions separately for each channel.
At inference, its standard procedure uses estimated population statistics instead of recomputing them from the current batch. [Ioffe and Szegedy (2015), Algorithms 1–2 and Section 3.2](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v37/ioffe15.pdf#page=3).
Consequently, changing the other examples in a training batch can change one example's normalized activations.
That dependency is absent when inference uses fixed statistics.

## LayerNorm Uses One Representation {#layernorm}

For a transformer token vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, LayerNorm computes statistics across its $d$ hidden coordinates.
Each token in each example has its own statistics:

$$
    \begin{aligned}
        \mu&=\frac1d\sum_jx_j,\\
        v&=\frac1d\sum_j(x_j-\mu)^2,\\
        y_j&=\gamma_j\frac{x_j-\mu}{\sqrt{v+\epsilon}}+\beta_j.
    \end{aligned}
$$

The trainable $\gamma$ and $\beta$ have one coordinate per normalized feature and are shared across examples and token positions.
Training and inference use the same normalization operation, without a running batch mean. [Ba et al. (2016), Sections 3 and 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06450).
The exact normalized axes are part of the architecture: “LayerNorm” alone does not specify every possible tensor layout.

## RMSNorm Scales without Centering {#rmsnorm}

RMSNorm divides each coordinate by the root mean square of the same vector.
A common form includes a numerical stabilizer and a learned gain:

$$
    \begin{aligned}
        r^2&=\frac1d\sum_jx_j^2,\\
        y_j&=\gamma_j\frac{x_j}{\sqrt{r^2+\epsilon}}.
    \end{aligned}
$$

It does not subtract the mean, so its output need not be centered at zero.
Its simpler computation retains rescaling invariance in the idealized zero-stabilizer setting, while giving up invariance to adding a common offset. [Zhang and Sennrich (2019), Section 3](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2019/file/1e8a19426224ca89e83cef47f1e7f53b-Paper.pdf#page=3).
This does not imply that subtracting a mean is inherently unstable or that RMSNorm always outperforms LayerNorm.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: RMS, variance, and an example"}
Expanding the variance gives

$$
    \begin{aligned}
        v&=\frac1d\sum_jx_j^2-\mu^2,\\
        r^2&=v+\mu^2.
    \end{aligned}
$$

Ignoring $\epsilon$ and taking unit gain and zero offset, consider $x=(1,3)$.
Its mean is $2$, variance is $1$, and mean square is $5$.
LayerNorm returns $(-1,1)$, while RMSNorm returns $(1,3)/\sqrt5$.
Adding $10$ to both input coordinates leaves the LayerNorm result unchanged but changes the RMSNorm result.
Multiplying the whole vector by a positive scalar cancels between numerator and denominator for both operations when $\epsilon=0$.
Finite $\epsilon$ makes this scale invariance approximate.
:::

## Connections {#connections}

[Quantile normalization](quantile-normalization.qmd) uses fixed training-data references to express physical coordinates in a model's numerical range.
[Attention](attention.qmd#projections) combines information from sequence positions; normalization changes the hidden vectors used within a transformer block.
[Token embeddings](representations.qmd#embeddings) supplies the hidden-coordinate representation used in the LayerNorm example.
[Representations](representations.qmd) connects hidden vectors to text, images, and physical inputs.
